Release Notes: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds + Predictive Mode h1. Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds + Predictive Mode (GA) *Release date:* 2025-09-12 This release adds customer-configurable autoscaling guardrails for *Redwood Dedicated* deployments (hard *min/max capacity bounds*) and an optional *Predictive* mode that pre-scales for known traffic ramps while preserving safety invariants and auditability. h2. What changed h3. 1) Customer-configurable autoscaling bounds (hard enforcement) You can now set *hard* per-deployment capacity bounds: * *Min capacity* (baseline): autoscaler will not scale below this value. * *Max capacity* (ceiling): autoscaler will not scale above this value. Bounds are enforced in the autoscaler loop via deterministic clamping: * We compute *requested desired capacity* (from reactive + optional predictive inputs). * We compute *bounded desired capacity* = clamp(requested_desired, min, max). * We persist/emit a reasoned decision record (requested vs bounded and why). h3. 2) Predictive mode (optional, bounded, with reactive override) When enabled, Predictive mode biases scale decisions using forecasted demand signals (e.g., time-of-day patterns and historical workload characteristics). Predictive mode is designed as a *bias*, not a replacement: * Reactive signals (queue depth / saturation) can override prediction when prediction is wrong. * All outcomes are still constrained by min/max bounds. * If forecasts are stale/unavailable, the autoscaler falls back to reactive behavior. h3. 3) Safety, stability, and failure-mode handling This release includes additional guardrails to reduce oscillation and prevent unsafe downscales: * Scale cooldowns + dampening (anti-oscillation) * Minimum step sizing for scale changes (where applicable) * Safe handling of missing/invalid predictive inputs (no scale-to-zero behavior)

Dedicated Autoscaling: SLO & Alerting Updates (Bounds + Predictive Mode) ## Summary This page defines SLO and alerting updates for **Redwood Dedicated autoscaling** after introducing: - **Customer-configurable min/max bounds** (hard constraints) - **Predictive scaling mode** (forecast-informed desired capacity), with reactive override where applicable The goal is to ensure on-call has *clear, actionable* indicators when: - A deployment is saturating due to hitting **max bound** - A deployment is **unable to meet min bound** due to regional capacity shortage - Predictive inputs are **stale/incorrect** and impacting performance - The autoscaler is **oscillating** or stuck This doc includes: - New SLIs/SLOs and how we measure them - Paging vs ticket alert rules and thresholds - Error budget / rollout policy for pilot → GA --- ## Scope **In scope** - Dedicated deployments with autoscaler policy enabled (bounds + optional predictive mode) - Autoscaler loop outcomes and capacity-policy evaluation outcomes - Fleet signals that affect serving performance: queue depth, saturation, and bound-hit conditions **Out of scope** - Request quality / model output correctness - Smart Routing behavior (covered in routing SLOs), except where routing consumes bounded-state signals --- ## Definitions **Desired replicas**: autoscaler computed desired capacity from signals (reactive + optional predictive) **Bounded desired replicas**: desired capacity after clamping to customer bounds and platform safety rules: - bounded_desired = clamp(desired, min_replicas, max_replicas) **Bound-hit**: when the clamp changes desired. - **max-bound hit**: desired > max_replicas - **min-bound hit**: desired < min_replicas **Unmet min**: when the system cannot provision to the *bounded desired* due to

Confirm guardrails are active - Cooldowns present - Minimum step sizing and dampening enabled 2) Look for “prediction flips” - Prediction changes direction frequently **Safe mitigations** - Disable predictive mode for the deployment (most reliable immediate mitigation): - `rw-admin dedicated scaling-policy set --deployment <id> --region <region> --predictive-mode off --reason "INC-#### mitigate oscillation"` - Increase scale-down cooldown (prefer over changing min unless customer explicitly requests) **Escalate** - Autoscaler team: Vanessa Ortiz / Keiko Yamamoto - If reproducible, attach decision logs + charts to ENG ticket ### Scenario G: “Scale to zero” concerns (should not happen) **Statement** Dedicated deployments with bounds should never scale below min_replicas. Additionally, null/absent predictions must not trigger unsafe downscales. If you observe current_replicas approaching 0: 1) Confirm min_replicas is not 0 (some test environments may allow min=0; enterprise Dedicated typically should not) 2) Verify bounded_desired is not below min 3) If bounded_desired < min, treat as a P0 bug and open incident Mitigation: - Set min_replicas to a safe value immediately (with audit reason) - Disable predictive mode ## Operational procedures ### How to collect a complete “autoscaling debug bundle” When escalating, include: - deployment_id, account_id, region, model route (if relevant) - Time window (UTC) of impact - Current policy values: min/max, cooldowns, predictive_mode, rollout flag state - Graph screenshots/exports for: - queue depth + oldest queued age - desired vs bounded vs current replicas - bound hit rate - prediction staleness + prediction vs actual - Last 50 autoscaler decisions (CLI output) - Any provisioning/allocator error

Dedicated Autoscaling Policy: Control Plane Schema + Console UX (Bounds & Predictive Mode) ## Summary This document specifies (1) the control plane schema and API surface for Dedicated autoscaling bounds and predictive scaling mode, and (2) the Redwood Console UX for configuring and observing these settings. Primary goals: - Let customers set hard, enforceable min/max capacity bounds per Dedicated deployment. - Provide optional predictive scaling that biases desired capacity up ahead of known ramps while preserving safety and deterministic behavior. - Preserve backward compatibility: no behavior change for existing deployments until explicitly enabled. Non-goals (in this design): - Cross-region predictive placement. - Contract negotiation workflows. - Fully automated procurement. --- ## Definitions - **Deployment**: A Dedicated customer-facing serving deployment (model + configuration) with an autoscaled replica set. - **Replica**: Unit of capacity for a deployment in the fleet autoscaler (implementation may map 1 replica to 1 GPU or 1 slice depending on SKU). - **Desired capacity**: Raw target computed by autoscaler from signals (reactive and/or predictive). - **Bounded desired capacity**: Desired clamped into [min_replicas, max_replicas]. This is the only value the autoscaler is allowed to enact. - **Predictive mode**: Optional additional signal source providing a forecasted target; reactive signals still apply and can override prediction, but bounds always apply. --- ## Control Plane Data Model ### High-level structure We add a new optional object on Dedicated deployments: - `scaling_policy` (nullable): customer-configurable policy that modifies/constraints autoscaler behavior. We intentionally separate: - **Customer-configured policy** (stored in control plane) - **Effective policy** (derived

mode guidance Recommend enabling predictive mode when: - Traffic ramps are regular (time-of-day/week), and - The customer’s pain is “latency during ramp,” and - They can tolerate minor overshoot in exchange for fewer queueing events. Recommend leaving predictive mode off when: - Workload is highly irregular with low historical signal, or - Customer is extremely cost sensitive and will treat overshoot as unacceptable. ## Common misconfigurations (and what to do) - **min > max**: invalid. Ask customer what they intended; correct to min <= max. - **max set below current baseline need**: results in chronic max-bound hit; recommend raising max or reducing demand. - **Cooldowns too short**: causes thrash; recommend longer scale-down cooldown. - **Timezone mismatch for scheduled/ramp expectations**: clarify customer local time vs deployment region time. - **Rapid repeated edits**: can make behavior appear “random.” Ask them to pause changes for one stabilization window. ## Escalation routing (internal) ### Severity guide - **P0 (page SRE now):** unmet min affecting production, widespread elevated queueing with max-bound hit across multiple customers, suspected platform ignoring max. - **P1:** single-customer sustained queueing with max-bound hit and strict SLA impact; predictive mode causing repeated oscillation; audit log discrepancies. - **P2:** configuration guidance, cost questions, minor overshoot concerns. ### Who to loop in - **SRE (Dedicated)**: unmet-min states, suspected fleet shortage, customer-visible degradation. - **Infra/Fleet autoscaling** (Vanessa Ortiz / Keiko Yamamoto team): bound enforcement behavior, oscillation, scale-event reason correctness. - **Platform Control Plane** (Ethan Park / Benji Okafor / Jordan Lee): policy schema, validation, RBAC,

evaluation + auditability is required For every autoscaler decision cycle (or at minimum every effective change), the system MUST record: - `requested_desired` - `bounded_desired` - Active bounds (`min_replicas`, `max_replicas`) - Signal inputs and reason codes (predictive_valid, reactive_overload, cooldown_blocked, min_unmet, max_hit) - Whether the decision resulted in a scale event These records must be queryable for enterprise support and compliance review. --- ## Definitions - **Replicas:** number of serving instances backing a Dedicated deployment (GPU-backed workers). - **Requested desired:** desired replica count before bounds enforcement. - **Bounded desired:** desired replica count after hard clamp to [min, max]. - **Reactive signals:** real-time metrics (queue depth, saturation/utilization, latency, error rate) feeding the autoscaler control loop. - **Predictive signals:** forecasted demand (time-of-day patterns, scheduled events, historical trends) producing a target capacity ahead of observed load. - **Overload condition:** sustained indicators that the system is under-provisioned (e.g., queue growth + saturation + latency regression). --- ## Precedence and conflict resolution (normative) ### Capacity computation sequence 1. Load effective scaling policy (post-validation). 2. Compute `reactive_desired`. 3. If predictive enabled and forecast valid, compute `predictive_desired`. 4. Compute `requested_desired`: - If overload critical: `requested_desired = max(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)` with overload step-up allowed. - Else: - For upward moves: `requested_desired = max(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)` - For downward moves: `requested_desired = min(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)` but blocked by scale-down safety rules. 5. Apply clamp to produce `bounded_desired`. 6. Apply cooldowns / dampening gates. 7. Emit decision record + metrics. ### Bounds enforcement is always last Bounds are applied after we compute requested desired, but

Autoscale Policy Safety and Fallback Playbook for Private Deployments Summary This playbook describes a conservative, telemetry-driven autoscaling policy and its associated safety gates and fallback procedures for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It focuses on protecting SLOs during scaling events, avoiding oscillation, preserving KV/prefix cache health for stateful inference runtimes, and providing clear rollback and escalation steps when autoscaling causes regressions. The guidance is applicable to both Dedicated and Private clusters that run the Redwood serving runtime. Scope - Applies to autoscaler configuration that controls GPU-backed inference pods and node pools in Private deployments. - Covers trigger signals (latency, queue depth, cache-hit ratio, memory pressure), safety gates, canary probing, fallbacks (model variant routing), and rollback procedures. - Out of scope: scheduling-level device allocation optimizations and hardware procurement. Goals and SLOs - Primary SLOs to defend during scaling: - Latency p50 < 150ms, p95 < 800ms for short-query workload (<= 256 tokens) - End-to-end error rate < 0.2% - Successful model initiation and warmup within 45s for cold-start model variants - Operational objectives: - Avoid autoscaler-driven latency regressions during scale-out/scale-in (target < 10% p95 variance during events) - Ensure at least 15% capacity headroom after autoscale completes for expected traffic spikes Definitions - Probe traffic: small, instrumented requests sent to new capacity to validate correctness and warm KV-cache. - Warmup window: time after a new replica is created during which we expect KV cache builds and initial model compilation to complete. - Model variant: a functionally equivalent model binary (quantized

with deployment region settings. - Avoid repeated manual edits; let the system stabilize. **Escalate if:** - Oscillation persists with reasonable cooldowns OR corresponds to known predictive-mode issues (see Known Issues page). ### 5) “We set min=10 but only see 6 replicas” Treat as **P0** if customer is production impacted. **Do:** - Confirm whether they are in an unmet-min state (capacity shortage). - Confirm region and time window; check if other accounts are affected. **Escalate immediately to:** - SRE on-call (Dedicated) + Infra fleet on-call **What to tell the customer:** - Acknowledge degraded baseline, provide ETA only if SRE supplies one. - Offer temporary mitigations if available (traffic shaping, shifting to another region if contractually allowed, lowering min only if customer agrees and it aligns with available capacity—do not unilaterally change policy). ## Guidance: how to choose min/max (recommendation playbook) Use this section for tickets like “How should we set bounds to meet our SLA?” ### Step 1: Determine objective constraints Ask: - What is the target p95 latency and error rate during peak? - What is the peak window duration and how fast does it ramp? - What is the maximum monthly spend or peak-day cap? - Is the application allowed to degrade gracefully at peak (fallback model, rate limiting, shedding)? ### Step 2: Recommend a starting min Principle: **Min should cover the first 5–15 minutes of the expected ramp** (or the time it takes reactive scaling to catch up), not the entire peak. We’ve engaged our on-call team and are actively working to restore capacity. We will provide updates as soon as we have confirmed progress or an ETA. Please share: - The time window(s) of the ramp (with timezone) - Any scheduled events - A screenshot of desired vs bounded replicas and queue depth during the event” ## Internal notes / do-not-do list - Do not promise specific capacity availability during region shortages. - Do not change customer scaling policy (min/max, predictive toggle) without explicit customer confirmation and a recorded ticket note. - Do not frame max-bound hit as a “platform failure”—it is usually expected behavior. - Avoid diagnosing solely from anecdotes; always anchor to desired vs bounded, bound-hit, and queue/saturation signals. ## Attachments and references - Dedicated autoscaler troubleshooting runbook (SRE/On-call) - Autoscaling bounds observability dashboard spec

Customer bounds are **hard constraints** on desired capacity For a Dedicated deployment with customer bounds: - Autoscaler MUST NOT set desired replicas below `min_replicas`. - Autoscaler MUST NOT set desired replicas above `max_replicas`. - Bounds apply regardless of the source of desired capacity (reactive, predictive, operator, or platform defaults). **Canonical clamp:** `bounded_desired = clamp(requested_desired, min_replicas, max_replicas)` Where: - `requested_desired` is the desired replica count computed prior to bounds enforcement. - `bounded_desired` is the desired replica count after applying hard bounds. ### D2. Precedence order for computing requested_desired The autoscaler computes `requested_desired` using the following precedence and arbitration rules: 1) **Hard safety overrides (scale-up only)** - If reactive overload signals exceed critical thresholds (e.g., sustained queue growth / saturation), autoscaler may request an *immediate* scale-up (subject to `max_replicas`). 2) **Predictive desired (if enabled and valid)** - If predictive mode is enabled and the forecast is “valid” (fresh, confidence >= minimum, model coverage OK), compute a predictive desired target. 3) **Reactive desired (always available)** - Compute reactive desired from observed metrics (queue depth, utilization/saturation, latency signals) using the standard control loop. 4) **Arbitration between predictive and reactive** - Requested desired is the **max()** of predictive and reactive desired for scale-up decisions. - For scale-down decisions, requested desired is the **min()** of predictive and reactive desired, *subject to scale-down safety

Based on the Dedicated Autoscaler Troubleshooting Runbook, the autoscaler must adhere to the following key safety invariants and semantics [1]:

* **Bounds are hard limits:** The autoscaler must never exceed the configured maximum capacity or scale below the minimum capacity (`bounded_desired = clamp(requested_desired, min_replicas, max_replicas)`) [1]. It is always considered a bug to intentionally set `desired > max` or `desired < min` [1].
* **Predictive is advisory, while reactive is authoritative when overloaded:** 
  * Predictive scaling may raise baseline capacity ahead of traffic ramps, but if reactive signals (such as queue depth or saturation) show overload, reactive scaling must override the prediction upward while still respecting the max bound [1].
  * If predictions are missing or stale, the autoscaler must safely fall back to reactive-only behavior [1].
* **Deterministic and auditable evaluation:** Policy evaluations and scaling decisions must be deterministic and auditable [1].

This beta focuses on: - Recommendations for **continuous batching** and **prefix/KV caching** settings - Estimates for: - **Savings** (e.g., $/day and %) - **Performance impact** (p50/p95 latency deltas) - A simple **risk level** (Low/Medium/High) with plain-language explanations - A “closed loop” that records what you viewed/dismissed/applied so we can improve suggestion quality Non-goals (beta): - Quantization recommendations UI (may be referenced, not surfaced as suggestions here) - Auto-applying changes without explicit confirmation and rollout controls - Any contractual/guaranteed savings claims --- ## Who this is for - ML/platform engineers responsible for inference economics (cost per token) and SLOs - Product engineers who own specific routes and need safe, incremental tuning You should *not* treat suggestions as guarantees. They are estimates based on observed workloads and conservative modeling. --- ## Requirements and prerequisites ### 1) Access / permissions You must have the **Optimize Suggestions: Read** permission for the org/project. If the page loads but suggestions don’t appear, see: “Troubleshooting → RBAC denied”. ### 2) Beta feature flag This view is gated by a beta feature flag. - Internal enablement: see “How to enable Suggestions beta feature flag” (linked in related pages) - Customer enablement: coordinated via Product +

enough data is collected. - In this beta, we prioritize standard Console-managed routes/models. Some custom or experimental configurations may be excluded. --- ## Telemetry requirements Optimization Suggestions depends on aggregated telemetry and cost attribution signals. To generate recommendations, we require: ### Minimum data signals - Request volume and concurrency (QPS, in-flight) - Latency distributions (p50/p95; at minimum enough to compute stable percentiles) - Token usage/cost attribution by route/model (input/output tokens) - Sequence length distribution (prompt + completion lengths) - Cache metrics where applicable (cache enabled state, hit rate/eligible rate, cacheable prefix characteristics) - Current batching/caching configuration values (to compute a delta) ### Minimum history - Typically **≥ 7 days** of representative traffic per route/model (some high-traffic routes may qualify sooner; low-traffic routes may require longer) ### Staleness behavior - Suggestions are recomputed on a scheduled cadence. The UI surfaces a **“stale as of”** timestamp when estimates are based on older telemetry. --- ## Access and permissions ### Beta access (feature flag) This release is behind a feature flag and is available only to beta-enabled orgs: - Feature flag: **optimize_suggestions_beta** ### RBAC Viewing suggestions requires the appropriate permission: - Scope: **optimize.suggestions:read** (or equivalent org role mapping) If a user sees an access denied state, verify role assignment and audit logs per the RBAC runbook. --- ## How to request access (private beta) To join the beta, customers should: 1) Contact their Redwood CSM, or 2) Open a Support request with subject: **“Optimization Suggestions Beta Access”** Include: - Org name / org

Optimize Suggestions Service (Batching/Caching) — Service Overview ## Summary The **Optimize Suggestions Service** produces actionable, conservative recommendations to reduce inference cost for Redwood customers. In the current beta scope, the service generates suggestions for: - **Batching configuration** (continuous batching / max batch tokens / queue delay) - **Caching configuration** (prefix/KV caching enablement and tuning) Suggestions are surfaced in the **Redwood Console → Optimize → Suggestions** and are designed to be: - **Explainable** (clear “why” and “how to apply”) - **Conservative** (avoid overpromising savings) - **Safe** (risk labels + guardrails; no auto-apply) This page describes architecture, data sources, compute cadence, interfaces, ownership, and failure modes. --- ## Scope and non-goals ### In scope (beta) - Suggestion generation for batching and caching - Savings estimates (cost delta, $/day and %) - Performance impact estimates (p50/p95 latency deltas) - Risk level (Low/Medium/High) with explanation - Suggestion freshness/staleness handling - RBAC-scoped API for Console consumption - Telemetry + funnel analytics instrumentation ### Not in scope (beta) - Quantization/profile recommendations UI (may exist in backend experiments but not returned to Console) - Automatic application of suggestions - Contractual savings commitments or billing reconciliation guarantees --- ## High-level architecture **Primary components** 1) **Telemetry ingestion & aggregates** (Platform Telemetry) - Collects request/response metrics and cost attribution signals. - Produces hourly and daily aggregates keyed by org/project/route/model/region. 2) **Suggestion compute job** (Optimize) - Periodically reads aggregates and generates candidate recommendations. - Runs estimator + risk scoring + guardrail filters. - Writes results to the Suggestions Store with stable

Optimization Suggestions (Beta): Guardrails, Safety Constraints, and Edge Cases ## Purpose This document defines **guardrails** and **constraints** used by the Optimize Suggestions system (beta) when generating **batching** and **caching** recommendations. The goal is to ensure that suggestions: - Are conservative and safe for production workloads. - Avoid recommending changes that are likely to violate latency/reliability SLOs. - Are robust to telemetry gaps and known workload edge cases. - Are explainable in the Console (“why we recommend this”, “what could go wrong”, and “how to apply safely”). This doc is normative for suggestion generation logic. If a recommendation is blocked by a hard guardrail, it should not be emitted. ## Scope (beta) In scope: - **Batching suggestions:** tuning continuous batching parameters (e.g., max_batch_size, max_batch_delay_ms, target_tokens_per_batch) for a specific route/model. - **Caching suggestions:** enabling or tuning prefix/KV caching parameters (e.g., cache enablement, cache capacity tier recommendations, cache admission policy). Out of scope (beta): - Quantization recommendations. - Automatic application of settings without user action + rollout controls. - Customer-specific savings guarantees. ## Definitions - **Route:** A customer-defined API route or application endpoint (often maps to model + prompt pattern + traffic). - **Suggestion unit:** (org_id, project_id, environment, region, route_id, model_id, model_version). - **Interactive route:** User-facing requests where tail latency is highly visible (chat UI, autocomplete, agent loops). - **Batching:** Combining multiple requests into a single forward pass window to improve GPU utilization; typically increases queueing. - **Caching:** Reusing computation for repeated prefixes/KV states; can reduce cost/latency when prompts share prefixes. - **Risk

This PRD describes the beta UX scope, requirements, success metrics, GA criteria, and staged rollout plan. --- ## Problem statement Customers know there are meaningful cost savings available via batching/caching tuning, but today: - It is hard to identify *where* cost is concentrated and *which* levers will help. - Teams don’t trust estimates without context (assumptions, confidence, and tradeoffs). - Engineers are cautious: “cost optimization” is often perceived as risky for latency SLOs or operational stability. We need a lightweight, credible interface that surfaces the best next actions and explains the expected outcome and risk. --- ## Goals (beta) 1) **Actionable recommendations** - Surface top batching/caching opportunities by route/model and provide direct links to relevant configuration pages. 2) **Trust and clarity** - Show estimated savings (absolute + %) and estimated performance impact (p50/p95 latency deltas) with clear assumptions. - Provide a simple risk level (Low/Medium/High) that

Risk level definition and UX copy guidelines (Optimization Suggestions beta) ## Purpose This document defines **Low / Medium / High** risk levels for Optimization Suggestions (beta) and provides **UX copy guidelines** for: - Risk badges and tooltips - “Why we recommend this” explanations - Disclaimers and guardrails language - Examples of user-facing copy for batching and caching suggestions This is for the Redwood Console **Suggestions** experience (batching + caching only) and is aligned with **Risk Scoring Model v0** (see related ADR). ## Scope and non-scope **In scope (beta):** - Risk labels for suggestions that change **batching** and/or **caching** behavior. - Risk as defined by **performance** and **reliability** impact. - Optional mention of **quality** only when it can be user-perceived (e.g., timeouts truncating responses), not model capability. **Out of scope:** - Security/compliance risk - Contractual or guaranteed savings - Quantization risk labeling (can be referenced but not shipped in this view) ## Definitions: what “risk” means in this UI In the Suggestions beta, **risk** represents the likelihood that applying the suggestion could cause a meaningful negative change to a route’s: - **Latency** (p50 / p95) - **Reliability** (timeouts, 5xx, queueing saturation, throttling) Risk is not a measure of “how scary” a change is; it is a conservative estimate based on telemetry + heuristics. ### Explicitly not included - **Security risk:** We do not imply that any suggestion changes data exposure or access control. - **Billing risk:** Risk is not about pricing uncertainty; savings are estimates with assumptions. - **Model quality risk

“Why we recommend this” section **Order:** 1) Opportunity summary (savings + what change) 2) Primary reason(s) (1–3 bullets) 3) Risk explanation (1–2 bullets) 4) What we monitored / assumptions (collapsed by default) 5) Guardrails and recommended rollout steps **Rules:** - Use **route-specific language** (“this route”) instead of generic (“your system”). - Tie claims to observable metrics (cache hit rate, concurrency, p95 tail) without dumping raw values. - Avoid blaming the customer (“Your config is wrong…”). Use neutral phrasing. ### 4) Disclaimers (must be present in details) Include a small “Estimates & limitations” block in the details drawer. **Required disclaimer copy (beta):** - “Savings and performance impact are estimates based on recent telemetry and may differ from actual results.” - “Risk reflects potential latency/reliability impact (not security risk).” - “Apply changes with canary rollout and monitor p95 latency and timeouts.” Optional, when relevant: - “Estimates may be less accurate for bursty traffic or if telemetry coverage is limited.” - “If your workload changed recently, allow time for telemetry to reflect the new pattern.” ### 5) “Risk” language do’s and don’ts **Do:** - Say “may increase p95 latency” not “will increase latency.” - Mention **timeouts** and **tail latency** as concrete outcomes. - Use “under peak load” when that is the driver. **Don’t:** - Mention “GPU” or internal infrastructure as the cause unless it helps the customer act. - Mention internal threshold numbers. - Use compliance/security terms (SOC2, HIPAA, PII) in risk badge copy. ## Rollout/guardrails copy (apply actions) Even though beta does

ADR: Suggestions API contract, stable suggestion IDs, and pagination (Console Suggestions beta) ## Status Published (effective for Console Suggestions beta). ## Context Redwood Console is shipping a beta “Optimization suggestions” experience focused on batching and caching recommendations. The Console needs a stable, predictable API contract so it can: - Render a list view with sorting/filtering and a details drawer. - Track user actions (impression/expand/dismiss/apply) against a stable identifier. - Support deep links and “dismissed” state that survives recomputation. - Handle pagination safely for large orgs/projects. The Optimize Suggestions service recomputes suggestions on a cadence (hourly/daily) based on telemetry aggregates. This creates inherent churn: suggestions may be added/removed and estimates may change even when the underlying opportunity is “the same.” Without stable IDs and a clear pagination strategy, the Console will show flicker, lose dismissals, and risk mis-attributing events. This ADR defines: 1) API shape (resource model and fields) 2) Stable suggestion ID scheme 3) Pagination/sorting strategy 4) Backward-compatibility requirements for the Console ## Decision ### 1) Endpoint and high-level contract We will expose a single list endpoint for the beta: **GET** `/v1/optimize/suggestions` The endpoint returns suggestions scoped to the caller’s org/project and permissions (RBAC enforced server-side). The Console is responsible for rendering and for linking out to the relevant config/apply workflow. ### Making Recommendations Actionable
* **Top opportunities per route and model:** Highlight the highest-impact batching and caching opportunities broken down by route and model [1].

### Building Trust and Clarity
* **Conservative savings estimates:** Present conservative estimates (avoiding overpromising savings) showing both absolute values (e.g., $/day) and percentages [1], [3], [4].

A binding always attaches to exactly one scope. Supported scope types: - **org:<org_id>** - **project:<project_id>** (must belong to an org) - **environment:<env_id>** (must belong to a project) - **cluster:<cluster_id>** (Dedicated/Private operational scope; cluster belongs to an environment) Scope inheritance: - A role binding at org scope applies to all descendant projects/environments/clusters within the org. - A binding at project scope applies to environments/clusters in that project. - A binding at environment scope applies to clusters within that environment. - Cluster scope is leaf. Constraints: - No cross-org inheritance. - “Global” scope is not exposed to customers. Based on the company documentation, the core authorization principles of RBAC v2 across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments include:

* **Least-Privilege Access and Separation of Duties:** Access is governed by a canonical catalog of fine-grained, explicit permissions where every sensitive action maps to an atomic permission string [1, 3]. Users or service identities are granted only the permissions required for their role, supporting clear separation of duties (e.g., separating Security Admins, Platform Operators, and Billing Admins) [2, 3].
* **Deny-by-Default:** Authorization is deny-by-default; if no explicit role binding grants a permission at the requested scope, the action is denied [1, 2]. Sensitive endpoints require explicit annotations/registrations to prevent unprotected endpoints from shipping [1].
* **Scoped Role Bindings and Inheritance:** Access is granted by binding roles to subjects at specific, hierarchical scopes [1, 2]:
  * **Org Scope:** Applies to the entire organization/tenant [1, 2].
  * **Project Scope:** Applies to a project/workspace within an org [1, 2].
  * **Environment Scope:** Applies to an environment (e.g., dev/staging/prod) within a project [1, 2].
  * **Cluster Scope:** Supported for Dedicated/Private operational and admin tasks as a leaf scope within an environment [1, 2].
  * Role bindings inherit downward to descendant scopes (Org → Project → Environment → Cluster), with no cross-org inheritance and no customer-facing "global" scope [1].
* **Consistent Enforcement Across Surfaces:** Authorization checks and error semantics are enforced consistently across the API Gateway (edge enforcement), Control Plane services (authoritative enforcement), and the Console/admin tooling [1, 7].
* **Enterprise-Grade Auditability:** Authorization decisions (both allows and denials) are structured and logged with context—including subject, action, resource, scope, policy version, and denial reason—and support export to SIEM systems for compliance and evidence [1, 2, 3].
* **Separation of Authentication and Authorization:** Authentication (handled via API keys, SSO, SAML, or OIDC) remains separate from authorization; identity provider (IdP) groups and identities are mapped to Redwood roles and scoped bindings [1, 2].
* **Reliability and Fail-Closed Behavior:** The system utilizes low-latency deterministic checks and safe caching, with defined fail-closed behavior for sensitive actions during partial outages [1].

It explains measurement primitives, benchmark designs, integration points with the EvalRunner harness, and regression triage steps when token-related regressions are detected. The goal is to make token cost and behavior first-class signals in model promotion and runtime configuration decisions.

Why this matters:
- Per-token cost is a major driver of customer unit economics and product UX.
- Small changes in generation behavior (longer prefixes, repeated tokens, verbose completions) compound across large volumes.

Purpose: This playbook defines the Priming Index — a compact, service-level artifact used to summarize context-priming sensitivity and per-slice fidelity risk for production prompt families. The Priming Index ties together prompt-set metadata, eval-harness measurements, quantization sensitivity vectors, and triage rules used during model rollouts and regression investigations.

Scope: Applied ML teams, model-onboarding leads, and SRE/ops responsible for rollout coordination. This is intended to be used during: onboarding -> shadowing -> canary -> general rollout and for triaging fidelity regressions post-deploy.

Quick summary of deliverables
- Priming Index JSON schema (compact metadata to live alongside model-version artifacts).
- Fidelity curation rubric (graded actions by index score).
- Eval-harness integration steps for measuring index components (sampling, seeds, and variance budget).
- Quant-sensitivity guidance: crosswalk between index bands and quant profiles.
- Regression triage playbook: escalation ladder, rollback gates, and automated blames.

Definitions
- Priming: any prompt or session history used to bias model output. Includes single-turn instructions and multi-turn system-state.
- Priming Index (PI): 0..100 integer that captures combined sensitivity across four axes: context-sensitivity, semantic-variance, token-economy exposure, and quant-fragility.
- Fidelity: operational measure of response correctness/coherence relative to golden annotations or slice-level metrics.

Index calculation (high-level)
1) For a given prompt-family, collect N = 1,000 stratified probes (from workload fingerprinting).
2) Run eval-harness under three conditions: baseline float32, target-quant, and simulated-prefix-loss.
3) Compute per-probe deltas: semantic-score-delta, embedding-stability-delta, length-token-delta, and nll-delta.
4) Normalize deltas per-axis to 0..1, weight axes (default weights: context 0.35, semantic 0.35, token-economy 0.15, quant 0.15) and sum -> PI (0..1) then scale to 0..100.

PI Banding and recommended actions

It provides a practical dashboard layout, metric definitions, alert rules (Prometheus/Grafana examples), and a lightweight investigation/runbook pattern to reduce false positives while enabling fast remediation. Background and motivation - Problem: LLM inference requests have widely varying token lengths and model behavior; a sudden change in average token-per-request (TPR) or in per-token latency can mask real regressions or cause spurious SLO burns. - Goal: Surface meaningful signals about token-level variability separately from model-quality/regression signals so operators can distinguish economic events (cost/throughput) from correctness events (quality). Key concepts and metrics - Token-per-request (TPR): tokens_total / requests_total (broken out by route/model). - Token variance (TPR_var): variance over a sliding 5m and 1h window to capture short vs sustained variability. - Token-burst ratio: 95th / median TPR per tenant or route. - Per-token latency: p50/p95 per_token_latency = latency_ms / tokens_in_request (use request-level deduped telemetry). - Token-cost-exposure: estimated_host_cost_per_token * tokens_total (derived from kernel/hardware cost profile). In the Token-Economy Evaluation and Benchmarking Playbook, the **Token Economy Index (TEI)** is defined as a composite score used to rank model variants based on their cost-quality tradeoff [1]. 

### Formula
$$\text{TEI} = (\text{normalized\_cost} \times \alpha) + (\text{quality\_penalty} \times \beta)$$
*(where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are configurable weights) [1].*

### Components
* **`normalized_cost`**: Calculated as $(\text{avg\_billable\_tokens} \times \text{per\_token\_price\_usd})$ and normalized to the range $[0, 1]$ across candidates [1].
* **`quality_penalty`**: Measured as $1 - \text{quality\_score}$ (derived from downstream evals), where the $\text{quality\_score}$ is within $[0, 1]$ [1].
* **Weights ($\alpha$ and $\beta$)**: 
  * **Default weights:** $\alpha = 0.6$, $\beta = 0.4$ [1].
  * **Adjustments:** $\alpha \to 0.7$ for latency-sensitive products, or $\beta \to 0.6$ for quality-sensitive products [1].

The goal is to provide a single authoritative workflow teams can run to certify that a code change, kernel rollout, or scheduler tune does not regress production SLOs.

Motivation and scope:
- Problem: We observe regressions that only appear when scheduler heuristics, kernel mappings, and telemetry interact under production-shaped load. Isolated microbenchmarks miss these interactions.

Runtime Energy-Aware Scheduling and Profiling Playbook Summary ------- This playbook documents our approach to energy- and power-aware kernel scheduling for the Redwood serving runtime, and prescribes a repeatable profiling and benchmarking workflow for validating energy-related optimizations. The goal is to reduce total energy per inference (Joules/token) while preserving latency SLOs and model-quality constraints. Scope ----- Applies to: the serving runtime (scheduler, kernel mapper, and dispatch layers) and the GPU-hotpath kernel implementations. Covers: telemetry, local and cluster-level scheduling policies, profiling methodology, benchmark scenarios, rollout recipes, and incident runbook steps for energy regressions. Does NOT replace thermal/firmware actions performed by cloud providers. Motivation ---------- - Our customer demand and operational costs require optimizing energy consumption for sustained workloads (e.g., embeddings, high-QPS chat). - Naive throughput maximization can increase energy per token due to inefficient kernel choices and poor batching alignment. - We need a documented, repeatable way to measure energy impact of runtime changes, and safe rollout patterns that respect latency SLOs. Goals and success criteria ------------------------- 1. Reduce median Joules/token for production embedding workloads by >=15% in targeted fleets without increasing p99 latency by >5%. 2. Establish an energy-profiling pipeline that provides reproducible per-kernel and per-request energy attribution within ±10% measurement error. 3. Add automated benchmark scenarios to CI that flag >10% regression in energy-per-token relative to baseline. Design overview --------------- At a high level we extend the runtime with three cooperating components: 1) Energy Estimator (lightweight): - Runs per-device and per-kernel cost models built from microbenchmarks (see Benchmark suite section).

The goal is to produce reproducible, SLO-driven measurements that connect observed token-level cost and latency back to routing/redispatch decisions, kernel scheduling characteristics, and model-variant selection. Results are used to validate cost-accounting telemetry, guide scheduler tuning, and certify fallback/redispatch policies before rollout. Audience: - Runtime engineers (kernel/scheduler) - Performance/benchmarking team - SRE and capacity planning - Product owners for routing and pricing Goals and success criteria: - Accurate attribution: >=95% of per-request cost is attributed to a provenance chain (routing -> model-variant -> kernel profile -> quantization profile). - Redispatch overhead measurement: measure median and 95th percentile end-to-end latency and token-cost delta introduced by redispatch within the runtime. - Sensitivity matrix: quantify how scheduler preemption, slot admission, and KV-cache eviction influence cost per token and end-user latency across three canonical workloads (chat, completions, and embeddings). - Benchmarks are automatable and checkpointed for regression detection in CI. Runtime scaling experiment protocol and benchmark checklist SUMMARY This page defines a repeatable experiment protocol and checklist for scaling experiments on the Redwood inference runtime. It combines workload construction, kernel scheduling knobs, telemetry targets, profiling hooks, acceptance criteria and rollback/runbook steps so teams can: (1) validate autoscaling/autotune changes, (2) quantify cost/latency trade-offs from scheduler/kernel changes, and (3) produce reproducible reports for release decisions. GOALS - Provide a canonical experiment recipe for both synthetic and production-replay workloads. - Make outcomes comparable across hardware generations and model families. - Capture actionable metrics: P50/P95/P99 latencies, tail token latency, per-kernel time breakdown, GPU SM utilization, memory pressure, and throughput vs. cost. SCOPE AND NON-SCOPE - Scope: inference-serving control plane + serving runtime up to kernel level (no downstream app logic). Includes KV cache behavior, batching, and preemption interactions. - Non-scope: training workloads, network fabric microbenchmarks outside the host (separate infra tests). Controlled Kernel Perturbation Playbook for Root-Cause Attribution Overview:

This playbook defines a controlled, repeatable experiment framework for perturbing kernel execution characteristics in the serving runtime to attribute latency, correctness, and fidelity regressions to kernel-level behavior. The goal is to support deterministic root-cause attribution for transient and steady-state regressions while preserving production SLOs and safety.

Who should use this document:
- Runtime engineers and system reliability engineers performing profiling or root-cause analysis.
- Kernel and scheduler owners validating changes to the kernel mapper, handoff, or fallback paths.
- Release engineers planning safety-guarded kernel rollouts.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: controlled perturbations of kernel latency, memory pressure injection, path toggles (fast-path vs fallback), and queue shaping for a selected tenant or shadow channel. Includes tooling, telemetry, safety checks, and interpretation heuristics.
- Non-goals: mass disruptive chaos testing at fleet scale (see accelerator-chaos playbook for those experiments); automated mutation testing of model weights.

Safety and approval checklist (required before any perturbation in a shared environment):
1) Perturbation run owner assigned and on-call notified.
2) Target workload scoped to a shadow/traffic-mirroring channel or single non-customer tenant.
3) SLA gate verified: choose experiments that guarantee p99 latency budget headroom >= 40% or use canary lane.
4) Runbook and rollback plan reviewed with SRE team.
5) Telemetry targets (metrics and dashboards) instrumented and smoke-tested.
6) Experiment window and blast radius (nodes, partitions) declared in the change ticket.
7) Emergency kill switch validated (runtime-dispatcher circuit-breaker to mute perturbation).

Latency slice synthesis and shadow benchmark specification Overview This document specifies the Latency Slice Synthesis (LSS) methodology and the Shadow Benchmark specification used by the benchmarking fleet to detect regression signals across model variants, kernel builds and scheduling policies. LSS is designed to produce reproducible latency cohorts ("slices") representative of production tail behavior while shadowing live traffic in a safe, low-impact manner. Goals - Produce stable, repeatable latency cohorts that expose kernel and scheduler regressions. - Provide a shadowing protocol that preserves customer privacy and complies with traffic quotas. - Define experiment automation, success criteria, and analysis artifacts for SRE/Runtime teams. Scope This spec applies to: hosted and dedicated runtime pools, synthetic replay harnesses, and the benchmarking fleet used during release gating. It intentionally excludes on-prem air-gapped installs (see onprem-packaging runbook). Key definitions - Latency slice: a cohort of requests grouped by features (sequence length, prompt entropy, model family, multi-turn vs single-turn) used to characterize latency distributions. - Shadow channel: a replicated execution path that runs concurrently with production but does not affect customer billing or responses. - Fidelity downgrade: intentional model/kernel setting reduction (quantization, reduced KV prefetch) used to measure graceful degradation behavior. If regressions are detected, revert using feature-flag rollback or scale down new variants. 6. Post-mortem experiment: reproduce with synthetic workload within 72 hours. Known issues (curated) --------------------- 1) Cohort oscillation under mixed bursty traffic - Symptom: cohort membership toggles for identical request fingerprints leading to cache fragmentation. - Probable root cause: fingerprint window too short (default 30s). - Mitigation: increase fingerprint stability window to 5 minutes for high-throughput cohorts; schedule a follow-up stability test. 2) Hedging-created duplicate kernel load - Symptom: hedged fast-path attempts increase GPU occupancy and raise queue times for best-effort cohorts. - Root cause: lack of cross-cohort hedging circuit-breaker. - Mitigation: enforce global_hedge_inflight limit and introduce per-node hedging accounting. 3) KV prefetch storm on rollout - Symptom: massive KV warmups when a variant is rolled out, causing transient I/O saturation. - Root cause: naive prefetch for all cohorts on deploy. - Mitigation: stagger kv_prefetch_window and use probabilistic prefetch sampling (10% initially). 4) Scheduler-ledger stale view after partial-network-partition - Symptom: admission decisions based on outdated credits causing over-admission. - Root cause: optimistic-local-ledger without timely reconciliation. - Mitigation: enable short reconciliation heartbeat (default 2s) and fall back

Econometric Latency-Cost Sensitivity Model and Simulation Runbook Summary: This document defines an econometric model for estimating how changes in runtime decisions (kernel selection, batching, quantization, routing) map to observed latency and per-token cost, and provides a reproducible simulation runbook for validating sensitivity hypotheses before production rollouts. Sandboxed Scheduler: Economic Admission & Canary Playbook Summary: This playbook documents the experimental scheduler sandbox (sched-sandbox) used to validate cost-aware admission policies, economic priority governor behaviors, and safe canary rollouts for kernel changes. It is intended for runtime engineers, oncall, and performance owners running safety-limited experiments against production-like traffic. Purpose and scope: - Reduce risk when introducing scheduler/econ changes by running them in an isolated decision plane that mirrors production inputs. - Capture SLO regressions, cost deltas, and fidelity impact before full rollout. - Provide a concrete runbook for activation, monitoring, rollback, and postmortem. High-level architecture overview: - sched-sandbox (service): an in-cluster decision plane that accepts a copy of dispatch metadata and returns admission/priority decisions for sampled traffic. It does not affect real dispatch; instead it annotates decisions for comparison. - kernel-admitter (component): produces observed kernel slot allocations and credits. Sandbox mirrors the API and uses the same kernel hints. - econ-governor (component): configurable economic model (weights for latency vs cost vs fidelity) used by sched-sandbox to synthesize priority. - profiling-agent: collects trace fragments, kernel timing, and cost estimates for sandboxed requests. Design principles: 1) Non-invasive: sandbox must never affect live routing or admission. Make-change-by-annotation only. 2) Deterministic inputs: ensure sampled requests have the same input features (sequence length, model variant, tenant tier, token budget). 3) Low-noise sampling: prefer stratified sampling by tenant and route to ensure representation across latency-sensitive and batchy workloads. 4) Telemetry parity: capture the same telemetry tags as production (kernel_id, slot_count, credit_charge, model_variant, origin_region). The goal is to ensure that shadowed traffic, synthetic probes, and production traces can be correlated end-to-end so that hallucination, latency, and quantization-sensitive regressions are attributable to concrete inputs and runtime conditions. Scope - Applies to all shadow deployments for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private modes. - Applies to evaluation harnesses that generate synthetic probes, load profiles, and edge-case fuzzing. - Does NOT replace per-model onboarding acceptance criteria; it augments traceability during continuous evaluation and rollouts. Shadowing & Fidelity Convergence Lab Protocol Summary This page documents the lab protocol for running controlled shadow (mirrored) traffic experiments to measure "fidelity convergence" across model variants and kernel scheduling profiles. Fidelity convergence is the process of comparing output quality (task-specific metrics and human-validated checks) between a live production model and candidate variants (quantized, distilled, or alternative kernels) while simultaneously measuring performance and scheduler interactions. The protocol is intended for benchmarking-and-perf-suite engineers, runtime engineers, and applied ML evaluators. Goals - Produce reproducible, comparable fidelity metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/EM/accuracy for task datasets; embedding cosine similarity for retrieval) between model variants and production model. - Measure kernel-scheduler interaction effects: how different scheduler policies (e.g., preemptive-shepherding, batch-slicing, slotting) affect fidelity under load. - Provide a safe failover and rollback runbook for experiments that impact latency or error budgets. - Deliver a data artifact package that supports triage: latency histograms, per-token cost, kernel trace events, KV-cache hit/miss rates, and sample outputs. Scope and Definitions - Shadowing: replicate a proportion p of production requests and send them to a candidate model variant without altering the client-visible response. Logging and sampling must ensure privacy and PII handling consistent with data policy. - Fidelity Convergence Threshold (FCT): threshold defining acceptable divergence; default: mean task metric drop <= 1.5% absolute and embedding cosine >= 0.985. Product teams can define stricter thresholds per SLA. - Kernel Scheduling Profile: a named set of scheduler parameters (slot_size, preemption_timeout_ms, batch_slice_limit) used by the runtime. Pre-requisites 1. Canary baseline: a validated production canary model id

Multifidelity Shadow Scheduler and Data Contract Overview Purpose This document defines the Multifidelity Shadow Scheduler (MSS) and the accompanying Data Contract used to reliably run shadow evaluations across heterogeneous fidelity levels (live shadow, synthetic micro‑probes, and replayed traffic). The goal is to provide a repeatable, auditable orchestration pattern that balances cost, signal quality, and safety for model promotion decisions. Scope - Applies to all shadow evaluation runs for inference-serving model variants (hosted, dedicated, private) that feed into promotion gates, regression triage, and quantization verification. - Describes scheduler behavior, fidelity tiers, data and telemetry contract, acceptance quorum, and runbook for promoting a shadowed candidate. Motivation As we increase the cadence of model updates and deploy quantized variants, teams need deterministic, cross‑region shadowing that: - Produces comparable signal across fidelity types, - Avoids overloading production paths, and - Provides a clear data contract so evaluators and SREs can reason about drift and regressions. Definitions - Fidelity levels: 'live' (mirror small percentage of live traffic), 'hybrid' (mixed live+synthetic), 'synthetic' (replayer or probe-driven), 'replay' (historical traffic playback). - Quorum: minimum aggregate of evaluator signals (numeric metrics and human review votes) required before a promotion decision. - Shadow run: an execution of a model variant in non‑serving mode where outputs are collected for evaluation only. Design overview - Scheduler is a central orchestration service (mss-service) that provisions shadow runs to runtimes (hosted/dedicated/private connectors). - Each run is assigned a fidelity class and a telemetry profile. - Data Contract guarantees schema, sampling, and retention for evaluation

Shadow Kernel Emulation Benchmark Protocol (SKEB) - 2026 Summary: This document defines the Shadow Kernel Emulation & Benchmark Protocol (SKEB): a standardized lab procedure, metrics contract, and release-gate checklist for evaluating experimental GPU kernel behavior using an emulator/shadow runtime prior to any production rollout. SKEB reduces risk from kernel regressions that affect tail latency, KV-cache correctness, and scheduling fairness by validating kernels in a controlled shadow environment that mirrors production traffic shapes. Goals and non-goals: - Goals: - Provide a repeatable protocol to compare a candidate kernel against the incumbent across cost, latency tails, and failure modes. - Surface subtle interactions between scheduler admission signals, KV cache warmup patterns, and kernel memory fragmentation. - Produce a deterministic artifact (bench report) to inform release gating and rollback criteria. - Non-goals: - This is not an exhaustive functional test suite for model correctness or model artifacts. - SKEB does not replace live canaries; it reduces the failure surface before canarying. When to run SKEB: 1. New kernel rollout (any kernel that modifies memory allocation, batching, or attention implementation). 2. Scheduler policy changes that alter admission or preemption behavior. 3. Quantization/backing-store changes that affect execution pathing. Overview of the protocol: - Step 0: Define the experiment matrix (workloads, sequence length distributions, model variants, concurrency shapes). - Step 1: Create a shadow-emulation environment that accepts production sampling traffic (mirrored or synthetic replay). - Step 2: Run incumbent kernel baseline experiments (N runs), collect metrics and traces. - Step 3: Run candidate kernel under identical

on model or runtime config and re-run shadow. Rollback criteria (immediate or automated): - Any critical safety failure (severity >= 4) observed in the shadow outputs. - Sustained p95 latency exceeding baseline + 100ms for >10 minutes. - GPU memory OOM or >95% sustained memory utilization for >5 minutes. - KV cache churn leading to cold-start amplification >25% over baseline. Triage and debugging playbook (on Yellow/Red): - Ownership: ML owner to lead quality triage; SRE to lead perf/memory; Safety SME to lead policy incidents. - Minimum artifact set to open triage ticket: failing request IDs, model build hash, runtime kernel tags, quant config, and raw model output (hashed + redacted as needed). - Standard steps: reproduce failure with isolated replay; narrow to minimal prompt; compare float vs quantized outputs; run profiler to capture kernel-level hot paths. Privacy and telemetry controls: - Shadow deployments must respect PII/data retention policies. Raw outputs used for triage must be hashed or redacted before storage. - Data collected during shadow is governed by the customer-specific confidentiality flag; for Private installs, default to restricted unless customer explicitly permits debug artifact sharing. Operational knobs and recommendations: - Use continuous batching profiles tuned for the target pool to avoid spurious latency regressions when sampling traffic. - Prefer paired inference (float vs candidate) for a statistically robust delta rather than absolute thresholds alone. - When validating quantized builds, include both microbench kernels and end-to-end user-level prompts in the same shadow window. Capacity stewardship cadence and SLO portfolio alignment Overview This document prescribes a repeatable cross-functional cadence for capacity stewardship that ensures the SLO portfolio is aligned with real capacity supply and business priorities. It focuses on continuous reconciliation of SLOs, error budgets, and multi-tenant capacity allocation (headroom) so teams can make predictable trade-offs between cost, latency, and availability. Goals - Maintain >=95% confidence that committed SLOs are achievable given current capacity commitments and forecasted demand. - Detect and remediate SLO drift and error-budget consumption early (target detection within 24 hours of significant change). - Provide a predictable, auditable cadence for capacity reallocation and non-disruptive migration of tenant traffic. Scope and audience This is intended for SREs, product/platform owners, and service stewards responsible for inference-serving and multi-tenant routing. Applies to hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments where central capacity governance is required. Key concepts and definitions - SLO portfolio: the set of active SLOs (latency, availability, correctness) across services that are eligible for central capacity stewardship. - Error budget: remaining fraction of SLO slack for a lookback window (typically 30d); used as the operational currency for throttles/rollouts. - Headroom: reserved capacity buffer (expressed in GPU-minutes or RPS-calc) to absorb short-term demand spikes without violating SLOs. - Stewardship window: the recurrent meeting where stewards reconcile portfolio health and allocate headroom (see Cadence). Shadow-to-Production: Eval Continuity & Safety Guidelines Summary:
This document prescribes the end-to-end process for using shadow (mirrored) traffic and continuous eval outputs to safely promote models into production for text generation and embedding workloads. It connects eval-harness artifacts (workload fingerprints, prompt coverage, quantization evaluation), runtime observability, and automated rollback triggers so teams can preserve quality SLOs while iterating quickly.

Goals:
- Ensure production promotions are gated by real-traffic shadow evaluation + synthetic continuity checks.
- Define concrete metrics, thresholds, and automated actions for safe rollback and triage.
- Provide runbook steps and ownership for degradation investigations spanning eval-harness -> runtime -> model-promotion-service.

Applicability:
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployment modes that support request mirroring (shadow routing).
- Target workloads: text-generation/chat, embeddings, and reranking.

Key Concepts and Signals:
1) Shadow run: mirror a sample of production requests to candidate model instances without affecting user-visible responses. Shadow traffic should preserve original request headers and sampling ratios.
2) Continuity test suite: a short, prioritized set of prompts derived from prompt-sets-and-benchmarks that exercise long-tail failure modes for the target workload.
3) Response Stability Index (RSI): a composite signal combining token-level edit distance, semantic-similarity delta (embedding cosine), and policy-safety flags. Range 0-100, lower is better.
4) Token Amplification Ratio (TAR): ratio of mean tokens generated by candidate model to baseline. Flags unbounded or degenerate generation.
5) Quantization Delta: measured difference in essential eval metrics (RSI, semantic-score, latency) between full-precision and quantized variants during shadow runs.

Gating Metrics and Thresholds (default baselines):
- RSI: <= 4.0 relative increase over baseline (if >4.0, fail gate).
- p95 latency: no more than 20%

Tenant-tail Sampling & Synthesized Probe Orchestrator Playbook Summary: This playbook describes the Tenant-tail Sampling & Synthesized Probe Orchestrator (TSPO): an operational pattern and reference implementation for safely sampling heavy-tailed tenant traffic, synthesizing privacy-safe probes for low-volume tenants, and projecting cost/impact prior to promotion to production evaluation or qual gates. TSPO addresses two recurrent issues: (1) noisy or sparse telemetry from rare tenants causing undercoverage of regressions, and (2) runaway evaluation costs when naive sampling pulls long-tail traffic at full fidelity. Goals and non-goals: - Goals: - Provide deterministic per-tenant sampling rules that preserve failure signal for heavy-tailed distributions while bounding eval spend to a configurable budget. - Allow automated generation of synthesized probes that mimic tenant context shape for low-volume tenants, preserving privacy and reducing data movement. - Expose cost-projection and acceptance thresholds to enable safe canary promotion. - Non-goals: - This playbook does not replace primary production telemetry (use SRE runbooks for production incident capture). - It is not intended for synthetic adversarial testing (use adversarial-probe-suite workflows). Definitions: - Tenant-tail: Tenants that contribute <X% of total request volume but account for disproportionate slice-specific failures or latency tails. - Synth-probe: A synthetic probe (input + expected metrics) generated from metadata + privacy-preserving aggregates to approximate a tenant workload. - Evaluation fidelity: The level of runtime parity with production (e.g., full model weights on Dedicated vs quantized shadow). SLOs and Budget Constraints: - Coverage SLO: 95% of tenant slices with historical failure-rate > 2x baseline must be represented in weekly probe

Instrumentation validation and synthetic traffic guidelines Summary: This document defines Redwood's standards for validating observability instrumentation using synthetic traffic and controlled signal injection. The goal is to ensure metric/tracing/log correctness, detect instrumentation regressions early, and keep production observability trustworthy as we evolve runtime, batching, and sampling behaviors. Scope: - Applies to all services owned by Redwood that emit metrics, traces, logs, or prompt telemetry to the centralized pipeline. - Includes hosted, dedicated, and private deployment flavors where we control the control-plane or can instrument agents. - Excludes third-party SaaS telemetry signals we do not control (those should have separate integration checks). Definitions: - Synthetic probe: a lightweight, deterministic client or agent that generates a repeatable set of requests intended to exercise specific instrumentation paths. - Signal integrity: correctness properties of telemetry (counts, histograms, span metadata, request IDs, tag values). - Whitebox vs blackbox probes: whitebox has access to internal headers/flags (e.g., kv-cache keys) to validate lineage; blackbox only observes external outputs. Principles: 1) Test in production with low-impact synthetic traffic. The most realistic validation runs against production services but must be rate-limited, tenant-aware, and labeled as synthetic. 2) Separate synthetic signals from user traffic at ingestion. Use explicit tags (telemetry.synthetic=true) and a durable provenance header (X-Redwood-Synthetic: probe/<probe-id>). 3) Fail closed on instrumentation contract violations. If a required essential metric is missing for >3 consecutive probe runs, escalate automatically (see Runbook). 4) Keep probes small and focused. Each probe validates a single hypothesis (e.g., histogram buckets, kv-cache hit labeling, trace-context propagation).

The goal is to produce an operational signal that directly informs traffic routing and automatic fallback policies in Redwood's smart routing layer. It covers metric definitions, workload synthesis, test harness configuration, pass/fail thresholds, and an incident triage runbook for latency regressions. Background and motivation: - Many customer-facing features require a sub-100ms median response time or predictable tail latency to maintain UX. - Model choices (size, quantization), runtime kernel selection, KV-cache hit patterns, and batching behavior all interact to create latency regressions that are invisible to token-count-only evaluations. - Automated routing and fallback should be driven by a reproducible eval signal that closely mimics production request characteristics. Scope: - Applies to: model variants intended for low-latency endpoints (chat-completion, single-turn generation with short context), runtime tunables that affect single-request latency (batching, prefetch, kernel/path selection), and routing/fallback policy parameters. - Excludes: large-batch throughput-only benchmarks, long-context (> 8k) full-document generation stress tests (covered by separate bench). Service-mesh impact and networked-fidelity benchmarks Overview This document captures the rationale, experiment design, sample configurations, and runbook for benchmarking how different service-mesh and network topologies affect inference fidelity and operational SLOs. It is intended for engineers running distributed Redwood Private or Dedicated clusters where network pathing (sidecars, mTLS, mesh proxies, ingress controllers) may interact with runtime components (frontends, routers, model shards, kvcache, and tracing). Why this matters - Network pathing can add microsecond-to-millisecond tail latency that changes batching behaviour and kernel scheduling decisions. - Proxies and sidecars may buffer, reorder, or aggregate requests which alters sequence arrival patterns and therefore KV cache hit rates and generation quality for stateful chat sessions. - mTLS and service-mesh observability can introduce CPU overhead on nodes hosting lightweight services and affect co-located scheduler performance. Scope - Topologies: direct (no mesh), mesh sidecar (Envoy-like), ingress+mesh (gateway + sidecar), and cross-region overlay. - Workloads: interactive chat (median tokens 40, tail 1024), streaming token-by-token generation, and bulk embeddings (batched). - Hardware: A40/RTX/T4 pools and mixed GPU pools used in Dedicated clusters. - Not covered: model-level quantization effects (handled in quantization-profiles). Success criteria / SLOs - Median generation latency (token emission) delta vs direct baseline <= 8% for interactive workloads. - 95th percentile latency delta <= 20% for streaming workloads. - KV cache hit-rate deviation <= 3 percentage points. - Fidelity regressions: BLEU/ROUGE-like drops or hallucination-rate increases must be <= 1.5% absolute vs baseline for canary pass. Scheduler integration and end-to-end profiling playbook Overview This playbook documents an end-to-end procedure for integrating scheduler-level signals with kernel and runtime profiling to diagnose performance regressions, validate scheduler changes, and produce deterministic benchmarking artifacts. It covers required telemetry, experiment templates, step-by-step collection recipes, analysis heuristics, SLO checks, and incident/runbook guidance. The intended audience is runtime engineers, scheduler authors, SREs, and performance QA. Scope and goals - Scope: production and staging runtime clusters, kernel scheduler variants (e.g., preemptive handoff, admission-controller tweaks), and profiling pipelines that touch GPU/CPU kernel execution, KV cache behavior, and request multiplexing. - Goals: - Provide a repeatable profiling and benchmarking workflow that links scheduler decisions -> kernel execution metrics -> end-to-end latency distribution. - Define minimal telemetry contract and collection commands so experiments are comparable across hardware and model variants. - Produce artifacts for regression triage (trace bundles, synthetic replay, and a short summary report). Surgical egress throttling for GPU workloads — operational playbook Overview:

This playbook describes surgical egress throttling patterns we use to protect multi-tenant GPU-serving capacity during network egress surges. It is intended for on-call infra, SREs supporting GPU pools, and platform engineers who operate egress proxies, NAT gateways, and Terraform modules that control tenant bandwidth and priorities.

Goals and scope:
- Maintain service availability for latency-sensitive inference workloads while containing egress cost and avoiding global network saturation.
- Provide a set of automated and manual mitigations that can be applied to individual tenants, tenant groups, or entire regions.
- Document Terraform and CI/CD patterns for rolling out throttling rules and testing them in lower environments.

When to use this playbook (trigger conditions):
1) System-level: total egress bytes/min by a region exceeds 85% of provisioned NAT/Egress capacity for 5m with sustained growth rate > 10%/5m.
2) GPU-pool impact: GPU tenant queue latency > SLO (95th percentile inference queuing > 200ms) and correlates with outbound bandwidth saturation.
3) Cost alert: burst egress spend acceleration exceeding forecasted daily budget threshold.

- infra.egress.bytes_per_minute.{region} (rollup by tenant_tag)
- infra.egress.nat_queue_length
- gpu.pool.queue_latency_p95
- gpu.tenant.active_sessions and gpu.tenant.kv_cache_hit_rate

- Per-tenant soft egress cap: 500 MB/min by default for shared GPU pools (configurable per tier).
- Per-tenant hard cap (emergency): 2 GB/min — requires manual approval or oncall action to raise.
- Regional NAT headroom: keep 20% free capacity for control-plane and system spike.
- Alert thresholds: trigger P0 when region egress > 95% for 3m and GPU-queue-latency_p95 >200ms.

Cross-tenant GPU Allocation, Fairness, and Preemption Strategy Overview Goal: Provide a clear, operational policy for allocating GPUs across mixed workloads (hosted inference, dedicated reserved pools, background training/batching, and internal experiments) that balances fairness, SLO compliance, and cost efficiency. This document describes the allocation hierarchy, preemption windows, eviction thresholds, terraform config patterns, monitoring/alerts, and an incident runbook. Context and motivation - Redwood operates a multi-tenant GPU fleet that must support: hosted API inference (low-latency, customer-facing), Dedicated reserved capacity (contracted throughput), asynchronous batch/embeddings jobs (throughput-optimized), and internal experiments (best-effort). - Historically we prioritized utilization and spot capacity, which increased customer impact during high demand spikes. This policy formalizes deterministic behavior to reduce customer-facing regressions. Principles 1) SLO-first for customer-facing workloads: Hosted API and Dedicated pools have top priority to meet latency SLOs. 2) Predictability: Preemption and fallback behavior must be deterministic and observable. 3) Fairness by intent: Teams with reserved capacity keep their guarantees; remaining capacity is apportioned by priority tiers and recent usage. 4) Cost-awareness: Prefer spot/spot-like nodes for best-effort work but provide safe fallbacks. Allocation hierarchy (high-level) 1. Reserved Dedicated Pools (contracted capacity) — absolute priority. 2. Hosted inference (hosted API / low-latency customers) — SLO backed, autoscaled. 3. Platform critical background work (model-serving warmup, cache rebuilds) — policy-controlled. 4. Best-effort batch (training, large embedding jobs, experiments) — preemptible on demand. Priority tiers and labels - reserved: dedicated_capacity (immutable to autoscaler decisions for other tenants) - hot: hosted_inference (SLO 95p latency target; non-preemptible except in extreme network/region failure) - platform:

Capacity Drills and SLO Recovery Cadence Playbook Overview:

This playbook defines a recurring cadence and concrete run procedures to: 1) test capacity assumptions proactively via capacity drills, 2) detect and arrest SLO burn during incidents, and 3) execute a structured post-incident SLO recovery and remediation plan. The objective is to reduce time-to-safe-state during SLO degradation, ensure repeatable capacity validation, and close the loop on technical debt that increases systemic risk.

Scope:
- Applies to all customer-facing inference endpoints (hosted API, dedicated pools, and private control-plane endpoints).
- Primary SRE owners: model-serving-oncall and capacity-engineering team.
- Secondary stakeholders: Product, Applied ML, Solutions, Customer Success.

Key terminology:
- SLO: measurable target (e.g., availability or p99 latency).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO over the rolling window (commonly 30d).
- Burn rate: rate at which error budget is consumed relative to baseline.
- Capacity drill: planned, controlled simulation of load or degradation to validate autoscaling, throttles, and fallbacks.

SLOs and thresholds (examples used in playbook):
- Availability SLO: 99.95% by count (30d rolling). Error budget = 0.05% of requests.
- Latency SLO: p99 < 600ms (inference token completion).
- Model health SLO: model correctness / quality sentinel failure rate < 0.5% per day.

Detection and telemetry requirements:
- Required dashboards: per-model SLO, per-route latency histogram, error-rate heatmap, capacity utilization by GPU pool, queue-length metrics, autoscaler actions log.
- Required alerts (examples):
 - slo-burn-warning: triggered when 30d burn rate > 1.5 for 6h.
 - slo-critical: triggered when rolling-window SLO < target for 10m or burn rate > 3 for 15m.
 - capacity-pool-saturation: GPU pool free-GPUs < 2 or avg queue length

Alert: Realtime SLO breach (SRE alert severity P2) — validate with query-trace for top 5 traces in last 5m. 2) If traces show KV cache thrashing or GPU memory OOMs: trigger node-evacuation playbook (see Node Evacuation Steps). 3) If high queuing but stable memory: enable thin_response policy for affected routes via runtime config and monitor 10m windows. 4) If fallback causing unacceptable quality regressions: revert and scale up Dedicated pool or open burst nodes in Hosted region. Node Evacuation Steps (automated and manual): Automated: - Mark node as draining in scheduler API: POST /internal/scheduler/nodes/{id}/drain - Migrate critical realtime-shares off node using live-migration hooks (or restart pods with preferred nodeAntiAffinity). Manual (if automation fails): 1) Notify owning team and call SRE runbook. 2) SSH to node and run: sudo systemctl stop redwood-inference-worker 3) Kill runaway processes: pkill -f "python.*inference_worker" (only after coordination). 4) Reboot node and run post-reboot health check: /usr/local/bin/redwood-node-health --check Rollout guidance for QoS changes: - Canary: start with 3% of capacity in a non-production customer pool for 48 hours. - Metrics to monitor: request p50/p95/p99, queue length, preemption count, node OOM events, customer error-rate, and cost-per-inference. - Automatic rollback: trigger if p99 increases by > 20% or customer error-rate increases by > 1% absolute within 4 hours. * **Connectivity Recovery SLO:** 99.9% of egress connectivity events recover within 60 seconds [5]. (The overall design goal is to provide sub-60s failover of tenant egress traffic during NAT/GW or peering failures [5].)

* **Upstream proxy 5xx rate (tenant tagged):** > 5% for 5 minutes (Priority: P1; Action: Failover to fallback proxy route) [1].

Adaptive Telemetry Bandwidth Management and Trace Priority Playbook Summary: This playbook defines the Adaptive Telemetry Bandwidth Management (ATBM) policy and Trace Priority model used by the Serving Runtime to keep observability useful under constrained telemetry budgets. It covers objectives, priority classes, runtime admission & backpressure behavior, operational controls, incident runbook, benchmark validation steps, rollout checklist, and known caveats. Goals: - Ensure high-value traces and metrics remain available when telemetry bandwidth is constrained. - Keep telemetry costs bounded while preserving the signal required for production debugging and SLA forensics. - Provide deterministic runtime behavior and simple operational levers for on-call and SRE teams. Background: Serving runtime produces three telemetry surfaces: kernel traces (per-kernel microtraces), request-execution traces (end-to-end per-request spans), and aggregated metrics/derived signals. Left unchecked, high request volumes or noisy customers can saturate export pipelines and storage. Terminology: - Telemetry budget (B_total): total egress capacity for observability (Mbps) assigned per region/cluster. - Priority class: categorization that determines sampling and propagation policy for individual traces/spans. - Trace score: runtime estimate (0-100) indicating the expected debugging value of a trace (hotpath errors, SLO breaches, anomalous latencies). - Backpressure window: sliding interval (default 60s) used to smooth admission decisions. Priority classes and default policies: 1) critical - Description: request traces associated with production 5xx errors, asserted SLA violations, security alerts. - Sampling rule: retain 100% of spans and full kernel trace payloads. No throttling. - Budget reserve: 35% of B_total. 2) high - Description: requests with tail-latency > P95 + configured delta or requests
